[2] The full recommendations were published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) on August 25, 2023. [6] These guidelines recommend routine annual flu vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications. [1, 5] Key updates for the season included a change in the vaccine's composition, specifically an updated influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 component for both egg-based and cell- or recombinant-based vaccines. [2, 5] Additionally, the recommendations were revised for individuals with egg allergies; it is no longer necessary for them to be vaccinated in special settings, and they may receive any flu vaccine that is appropriate for their age and health status. [2, 8] <5> The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) voted on its recommendations for the 2023-2024 influenza season during its meeting on June 21-22, 2023. The recommendations for the timing of vaccination remained unchanged, with September and October being the ideal months for most people to get vaccinated to prevent waning immunity. The finalized recommendations and updates were officially published by the CDC in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) on August 25, 2023. <6> The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has updated its recommendations for the 2023-2024 influenza season regarding flu vaccinations for individuals with egg allergies. [1] According to the revised guidelines, people with a history of egg allergy, regardless of the severity of their past reaction, can receive any licensed, age-appropriate flu vaccine. [2, 4] The previous precaution, which suggested that individuals with severe egg allergies be vaccinated in a medical setting supervised by a healthcare provider able to manage severe allergic reactions, is no longer recommended. [3] Instead, the updated guidance states that an egg allergy alone does not require any safety measures beyond the standard protocols for any vaccine recipient. [3, 4] All vaccinations should, however, be administered in settings equipped to handle potential acute hypersensitivity reactions. [3, 4] <7> In a Q&A published by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health on July 31, 2023, virologist Andrew Pekosz, PhD, predicted that the 2023–2024 flu vaccine would likely become available at the end of August 2023. [5] He recommended that the ideal time for most people to get vaccinated would be September or October, as this window would provide immunity for an early flu season and maintain protection if the flu emerged later in the winter. [5] The CDC also identified September and October as the best times for most people to get vaccinated. [6] For the 2023-2024 season, vaccine manufacturers projected supplying between 156.2 million and 170 million doses in the United States. [8] <8> CSL Seqirus, one of the world's largest influenza vaccine companies, announced on July 17, 2023, that it had commenced shipping its portfolio of influenza vaccines for the 2023/2024 U.S. flu season. [1, 2, 3] The company plans to supply over 55 million doses, which include its innovative cell-based, adjuvanted, and egg-based vaccine options for individuals aged six months and older. [1, 4] The announcement highlighted the significant drop in immunization rates since the COVID-19 pandemic and the potential for a severe flu season, referencing high influenza activity in the Southern Hemisphere as a predictor. [1, 3] <9> On March 7, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC) convened to select the virus strains for the 2023-2024 seasonal flu vaccines in the United States. [1, 2, 3] The committee recommended updating the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 component for all vaccines. [6] For egg-based quadrivalent vaccines, the committee recommended an A/Victoria/4897/2022 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus. [1, 4] For cell- or recombinant-based quadrivalent vaccines, the recommendation was for an A/Wisconsin/67/2022 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus.
